title: Chapter 29 Quiz — LLM Inference & KV Cache

questions.question: A decoder has 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, and stores keys and values in fp16 (2 bytes per value). How many KiB of KV cache does one token occupy?
questions.explanation: Per token: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB. Using 32 query heads instead of 8 KV heads would give 512 KiB, and storing fp32 would give 256 KiB.

questions.question: A request of 1,000 tokens is stored in pages of 16 slots. How many slots in its last page are empty?
questions.explanation: The request needs ⌈1000 / 16⌉ = 63 pages, which hold 63 × 16 = 1,008 slots. So 8 slots are empty.

questions.question: In the bandwidth-bound model for a 7B-class multi-head attention configuration at 4,096 tokens, the ceiling is 949 tokens per second at batch 32. If the batch is raised to 64, what happens to the ceiling?

options.text: It stays at about 949 tokens per second, and achieved throughput moves toward it
It doubles to about 1,898 tokens per second
It halves, because each sequence reads its cache twice
It falls, because larger batches add more cache reads per token

questions.explanation: The ceiling is BW / M_seq, where M_seq is the cache of one sequence. It does not depend on the batch size. The batch amortises the weight reads, so achieved throughput rises toward the ceiling but never exceeds it.

questions.question: Two parallel samples share a partly filled page. Someone removes the branch that copies a shared last page before writing. What goes wrong?

options.text: The memory use doubles, but every output is still correct
The attention scores are computed in the wrong order
The block table is rebuilt with one page per token, so the output is slower but unchanged
Both samples write their next token into the same slot, so each reads the other's token

questions.explanation: Without the copy, the two outputs share one physical slot. The second write overwrites the first, so the output depends on the other sample without any error being raised. The fix is to copy a shared partial page before writing into it.

questions.question: A sequence has block table [0, 2, 4] with page size B = 4. Token 9 is stored in which flat index of the pool array reshaped to (-1, 4)?
questions.explanation: Token 9 is in logical page ⌊9 / 4⌋ = 2, slot 9 mod 4 = 1. The block table maps logical page 2 to physical page 4, so the flat index is 4 × 4 + 1 = 17.

questions.question: The target distribution is p = [0.40, 0.10, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10] and the draft distribution is q = [0.20, 0.30, 0.20, 0.15, 0.15]. What is the overall acceptance rate β = Σₓ min(p(x), q(x))?
questions.explanation: min(p, q) = [0.20, 0.10, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10], which sums to 0.75. The rejected mass is 1 − β = 0.25, which equals the sum of max(0, p − q).

questions.question: Speculative decoding uses a per-token acceptance rate α = 0.8, draft length γ = 4, and a draft step that costs c = 0.1 of a target step. What is the modelled speedup, using E / (γc + 1) with E = (1 − α^(γ+1)) / (1 − α)?
questions.explanation: E = (1 − 0.8⁵) / 0.2 = 3.36 tokens per round. The round costs γc + 1 = 1.4 target steps, so the modelled speedup is 3.36 / 1.4 ≈ 2.40. The answer 3.36 forgets the cost of the draft steps. The formula assumes independent acceptance and a memory-bound target.

questions.question: Why does the acceptance rule that accepts a draft token with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)), and resamples a rejected token from max(0, p − q) normalised, leave the output distribution equal to the target's p?

options.text: Accepted draft mass for token x is min(p(x), q(x)), and replacement mass is max(0, p(x) − q(x)); together they sum to p(x)
The draft is always rejected when q(x) is larger than p(x), so the draft never changes the output
The draft distribution is replaced by the target after the first rejection, so later tokens are exact
Averaging over many rounds makes any acceptance rule unbiased

questions.explanation: Accepting x as a draft token has probability q(x) × min(1, p(x)/q(x)) = min(p(x), q(x)). A rejection leads to a replacement with probability (1 − β) × max(0, p − q) / (1 − β) = max(0, p(x) − q(x)). Adding the two gives p(x). This is the single-position argument, and the lesson checks it numerically.

questions.question: In the Medusa toy from Lesson 29.3, the context is token 9, the base token is 3, and the target's greedy chain is [3, 5, 6, 7]. Head 1 guesses 5, head 2 guesses 6 and head 3 guesses 7, each among its top-2 choices. How many tokens does one target call emit?
questions.explanation: All three guesses match the chain, so the accepted run is 3 tokens. The base token 3 is always correct, so the call emits the base token plus the three accepted guesses, which is 4 tokens. The lesson's code reports the same count.
